name: Polysilicone-15

lead: Polysilicone-15 is a large silicone-based UVB filter sold as Parsol SLX. It is used in sunscreens, lip balms and some hair products, so people can protect skin, lips and colour-treated hair from sun damage.

It absorbs UVB light with a maximum near 310 nm, and its polymer-like size is intended to keep it on the skin's surface. An in vitro study covered it among 18 EU filters, and published safety data are limited to a few case reports.

paras: It is applied as part of a sunscreen, lip balm with SPF, or hair product, usually combined with other filters. It is approved in the EU.
Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis and cheilitis. No controlled clinical trials are documented.

chain: Less UV damage to skin and lips
angle.text: Polysilicone-15 (Parsol SLX) is a UVB filter used in EU sunscreens, lip balms and hair products, so users can protect skin, lips and colour-treated hair from sun. Less UV damage supports skin that ages more slowly. Published work is formulation data and case reports rather than appearance trials.

lead: Polysilicone-15 (dimethicodiethylbenzalmalonate; trade name Parsol SLX, from DSM) is a siloxane-based oligomer used as a UVB filter that helps protect skin from sunburn and sun-related ageing, with peak absorption near 310 nm.[1] It is a colourless to pale-yellow liquid, practically insoluble in water.[1] It is approved for sunscreens and cosmetics in the EU, and appears in hair products such as shampoos, sprays and colour treatments.[1] It also appears in US-listed lip-balm sunscreens combined with other filters.[2]

For appearance, it is one of the filters that let a product protect against the sun. The US FDA says sunscreen helps prevent sunburn and may reduce the risks of skin cancer and early skin aging, and Wikipedia describes daily broad-spectrum sunscreen as slowing or temporarily preventing wrinkles, dark spots and sagging [3][4]. Polysilicone-15 covers the UVB range only, so formulas pair it with a UVA filter [2][5].

An in vitro study of 18 EU-authorised filters examined how filter concentration affects measured SPF.[6] Case reports describe allergic contact reactions to polysilicone-15 in a lip balm and in a sunscreen cream.[7][8]
In formulations it is typically paired with other filters such as the UVA filter butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, as seen in patents for sunscreen emulsions and in a US-listed lip balm [2][5][9].

paras: It is used in sunscreens, lip balms and hair-care products to absorb UVB.[1][2] A US-listed sunscreen lip balm combines it with ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, homosalate, octocrylene and butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, with label claims of helping prevent sunburn when used with other sun-protection measures.[2]

Patent filings describe oil-in-water sunscreen emulsions combining polysilicone-15 with dibenzoylmethane UVA filters, water-soluble UV filters and stabilising ingredients, and a shampoo containing microcapsules filled with UV-protecting ingredients and fragrance to prolong protection on hair and scalp [5][9][10].

Sunscreen active ingredients divide into organic filters, which absorb UV and release the energy as heat, and mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, which absorb, reflect and scatter light [4]. The SPF rating measures protection against UVB, the main cause of sunburn, while UVA contributes to deeper skin damage, which is why broad-spectrum products combine filters [3][4]. Polysilicone-15 belongs to the organic UVB group [1].

Polysilicone-15 (INCI name; chemical name dimethicodiethylbenzalmalonate) attaches benzalmalonate chromophores to a polysiloxane backbone. Wikipedia lists it as a colourless to pale-yellow liquid that is practically insoluble in water, with absorption peaking near 310 nm in the UVB range [1]. Absorbed UV energy is dissipated by the chromophore, so less reaches the skin.

In the EU, sunscreens are regulated as cosmetics, with minimum requirements that include an SPF of at least 6 and a UVA/UVB protection ratio of at least one-third, whereas in the US they are over-the-counter drugs, and a US-listed sunscreen lip balm containing polysilicone-15 appears on the DailyMed label database [2][4]. The FDA notes that sunscreens that are not broad spectrum or have an SPF below 15 must carry a warning that they only help prevent sunburn, not skin cancer or early skin aging [3]. Patent filings describe polysilicone-15 in compositions aimed at higher SPF, antioxidant potential, foundation make-up and hair care, usually in combination with other filters [5][9][10]. Marketing of the compound is attributed to DSM under the name Parsol SLX [1].

An in vitro study of 18 filters authorised in the EU first adapted its method by determining that 15 mg of product on a PMMA plate best matched in vivo results, then ranked the filters at the highest concentration allowed by European law. Polysilicone-15 gave an SPF of 3.64, comparable with oxybenzone at 3.01 and octylsalicylate at 3.12, while the highest values were for anisotriazine at 20.0, isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate at 15.14 and diethylhexylbutamidotriazone at 12.58 [6]. Because sunscreens combine several filters, a single-filter value describes its contribution rather than the finished product.

Allergic contact cheilitis from polysilicone-15 in a lip-care balm was reported in 2014, and allergic contact dermatitis involving polysilicone-15 and another filter (Tinosorb S) in a sunscreen cream was reported in 2022 [7][8]. Both are published as individual case reports.
No controlled clinical trials found. Evidence consists of an in vitro SPF study covering 18 EU-authorised filters and individual case reports of contact allergy.[6][7][8]
